title: Join related records
summary: A join matches records using a rule. It can show an author name beside a title without repeating that name in every book record.
introduction: A join matches records using a rule. It can show an author name beside a title without repeating that name in every book record. Your task: Add one more matching author and book.
learningObjectives: Add one more matching author and book.
Explain the example for join related records

blocks.text: A join matches records using a rule. It can show an author name beside a title without repeating that name in every book record.
Use the SQL Run button for examples marked runnable. They use this site's in-browser SQLite database and sample-only table names. A Python example needs Python on your own computer instead.

blocks.code:
WITH authors(id,name) AS (VALUES(1,'Mia')),books(title,author_id) AS (VALUES('Moon Trip',1))
SELECT books.title,authors.name FROM books JOIN authors ON authors.id=books.author_id;
blocks.title: Join related records

blocks.text: Read the code step by step

items: `SELECT` names the output values. `AS` can give a calculated result a readable column name.

blocks.text: The result pairs Moon Trip with Mia.

blocks.title: A mistake to avoid
blocks.text: A missing or wrong join rule can make extra combinations. Check with a tiny dataset first.

blocks.text: Add one more matching author and book.
